# Within-Person Dynamics {.appendix #apx-within-person-dynamics}
Having established that 3D stimuli elicit a clear angular disparity effect while 2D stimuli do to a lesser extent, we next asked a complementary question: whether children show sensitivity to task demands as they unfold in real time — specifically, whether reaction times shift systematically at the transition from 2D to 3D stimuli, and whether practice effects are detectable within blocks. To isolate time-on-task effects from item-driven RT changes, we residualized log-RTs on angle, stimulus, and item type prior to analysis.
```{r}
#| label: fig-within-person-trials
#| fig-cap: "**Trial-level Reaction Time Dynamics (angle-residualised).** Mean residual log-RT across trials for each non-adaptive site ±SE. The dashed line marks the 2D→3D transition. Re-test and CAT data removed."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

# prep: remove CAT data
trial_resid_data <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  filter(!adaptive, correct == 1)

# residualize log_rt on angle + stimulus + item_group
resid_model <- lm(log_rt ~ angle + stimulus + item_group, 
                  data = trial_resid_data)

trial_resid_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  mutate(log_rt_resid = residuals(resid_model),
         block = item_group |> str_to_upper())

transition_trial <- trial_resid_data |>
  filter(item_group == "3d") |>
  pull(trial_number) |>
  min()

# plot
ggplot(trial_resid_data, 
       aes(x = trial_number, y = log_rt_resid, 
           color = site_label, fill = site_label)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = interaction(site_label, block)),
              method = "loess", span = 0.75, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = transition_trial - 0.5, linetype = "dashed",
             color = pal$grey, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = transition_trial, y = Inf,
           label = "Start of 3D block", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  labs(
    x     = "Trial Number",
    y     = "Residual reaction time",
    color = "Site",
    fill  = "Site"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: within-person-models
#| include: false

# center trial number within each block so the intercept at transition is interpretable
within_person_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  mutate(
    block         = factor(block, levels = c("2D", "3D")),
    # trial number centered within block
    trial_c       = trial_number - transition_trial,
    site          = factor(site)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(trial_number), !is.na(log_rt_resid))

# Model 1: continuous trial slope only 
m_wp_continuous <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 2: add block as main effect — tests for discontinuous jump at transition
m_wp_jump <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + block + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 3: add trial × block interaction — tests whether slope changes after transition
m_wp_slope <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c * block + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# model comparisons
anova_wp_jump  <- anova(m_wp_continuous, m_wp_jump)   # is there a jump?
anova_wp_slope <- anova(m_wp_jump, m_wp_slope)         # does slope also change?

# extract key numbers
wp_coefs       <- coef(summary(m_wp_slope))

# block jump (intercept shift at transition)
beta_wp_block  <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_block    <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_block     <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# within-block trial slope (2D block)
beta_wp_trial  <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Estimate"]
se_wp_trial    <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_trial     <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# interaction: does slope differ in 3D block?
beta_wp_int    <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_int      <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_int       <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# anova numbers for inline reporting
wp_jump_chisq  <- anova_wp_jump$Chisq[2]
wp_jump_df     <- anova_wp_jump$Df[2]
wp_jump_p      <- anova_wp_jump[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]

wp_slope_chisq <- anova_wp_slope$Chisq[2]
wp_slope_df    <- anova_wp_slope$Df[2]
wp_slope_p     <- anova_wp_slope[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]
```

\clearpage

@fig-within-person-trials plots mean residual log-RT across trials for each site. To test for a discontinuous shift in RT at the 2D→3D block transition and for within-block practice effects, we fitted a series of mixed-effects models predicting residual log-RT from trial number, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes.

First, a model including a block indicator (2D vs 3D) significantly improved fit over a continuous trial-slope model (χ²(`r wp_jump_df`) = `r round(wp_jump_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_jump_p)`), confirming that the increase in RT at the 2D→3D transition is discontinuous rather than a continuation of a gradual trend. The block coefficient indicates a sudden upward shift in residual RT at trial 48 (β = `r round(beta_wp_block, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_block, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_block)`), consistent with children recalibrating their processing demands at the block boundary rather than adapting incrementally.

Second, within each block, RTs decreased across trials, indicating a practice effect operating independently of angular disparity (β = `r round(beta_wp_trial, 4)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_trial, 4)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_trial)`). Adding a trial × block interaction `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, "significantly improved model fit", "did not significantly improve model fit")` (χ²(`r wp_slope_df`) = `r round(wp_slope_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_slope_p)`) `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, paste0(", with the within-block acceleration differing between the 2D and 3D blocks (β = ", round(beta_wp_int, 3), ", SE = ", round(se_wp_int, 3), ", p ", fmt_p(p_wp_int), ")"), "")`. Both patterns — the discontinuous block transition and the within-block acceleration — were qualitatively consistent across all three sites, further extending the cross-cultural consistency observed in the angular disparity analysis.

# Cluster Solution Validation {.appendix #apx-cluster}

To assess the appropriateness of the three-profile solution, we evaluated cluster quality across k = 1–8 using two complementary metrics: total within-cluster sum of squares (the elbow method) and average silhouette width (@fig-k-sweep-validation). The silhouette analysis identified k = 2 as the statistically optimal solution, with average silhouette width peaking at 0.35 before declining steeply at k = 3 and remaining low thereafter. The elbow plot showed a moderate inflection at k = 3, after which additional clusters yielded diminishing reductions in within-cluster variance. To examine whether k = 2 was substantively adequate, we examined the RT–angle functions of the resulting two-cluster solution (@fig-k2-cluster-check). The higher-ability cluster displayed a characteristic inverted-U RT function, rising to a peak around 120° before declining at 160° — a pattern that, in the three-cluster solution, distinguishes the Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) and Mental Rotation groups. This indicates that k = 2 collapses two distinguishable effective engagement profiles into a single region, obscuring a theoretically meaningful behavioral difference. We therefore adopted k = 3 on both empirical grounds (the elbow inflection) and theoretical grounds (the interpretability of the resulting RT profiles), noting that the three profiles are treated as convenient descriptive anchors along a continuum rather than evidence for discrete strategy types.

```{r}
#| label: fig-k-sweep-validation
#| eval: true
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "**Cluster validation metrics: Elbow Method (left) and Silhouette Analysis (right).** The elbow plot shows a bend at k=3, and silhouette width peaks at k=2 before declining, providing partial support for the 3-cluster solution."

p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = 2, color = pal$red) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters k")

p_sil <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters k")

grid.arrange(p_elbow, p_sil, nrow = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-k2-cluster-check
#| eval: true
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**RT–angle functions for the k=2 cluster solution.** The higher-ability cluster displays an inverted-U RT curve consistent with a mix of Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching strategies, suggesting that k=2 collapses two qualitatively distinct effective strategies into a single group."

# --- 1. Set up Input (Same as before, removing Learning_Rate for clarity) ---
analysis_data_k2 <- rich_features_final %>%
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Baseline_Speed, Abs_Slope, Rel_Slope, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

global_input_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 %>%
  select(Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Instability, Abs_Slope, Learning_Rate) %>%
  scale()

# --- 2. Run K-Means with K=2 ---
set.seed(123)
k_global_2 <- kmeans(global_input_k2, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
analysis_data_k2$Global_Cluster <- as.factor(k_global_2$cluster)

# --- 3. Label the 2 Clusters ---
# We define them simply by Ability (Low vs High) since we can't split by slope yet
cluster_stats_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 %>%
  group_by(Global_Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_ability = mean(ability), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Identify Lower Ability Cluster
low_eff_id <- cluster_stats_k2 %>% arrange(mean_ability) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)
# The other one is High Efficiency
high_eff_id <- cluster_stats_k2 %>% arrange(desc(mean_ability)) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)

analysis_data_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 %>%
  mutate(Strategy_Label = case_when(
    Global_Cluster == low_eff_id ~ "Low Efficiency (Cluster 1)",
    Global_Cluster == high_eff_id ~ "High Efficiency (Cluster 2)"
  ))

k2_colors <- c(
  "Low Efficiency (Cluster 1)"  = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[1],
  "High Efficiency (Cluster 2)" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[2]
)

# --- 4. Plot the Curves (Visual Check) ---
# Join labels to raw data
rt_by_strategy_k2 <- mrot_rich_data %>%
  left_join(
    analysis_data_k2 %>% select(run_id, Strategy_Label),
    by = c("run_id")
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Label), is.finite(log_rt), is.finite(angle))

# Calculate User Means
rt_user_angle_k2 <- rt_by_strategy_k2 %>%
  group_by(Strategy_Label, run_id, angle) %>%
  summarise(user_mean_log_rt = mean(log_rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Calculate Group Means
rt_summary_k2 <- rt_user_angle_k2 %>%
  group_by(Strategy_Label, angle) %>%
  summarise(
    n_users     = n_distinct(run_id),
    mean_log_rt = mean(user_mean_log_rt, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_log_rt   = sd(user_mean_log_rt, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_users),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# plot
ggplot(rt_summary_k2, aes(x = angle, y = mean_log_rt, colour = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_log_rt - 1.96*se_log_rt, 
                  ymax = mean_log_rt + 1.96*se_log_rt, 
                  fill = Strategy_Label), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = k2_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = k2_colors) +
  labs(
    title    = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL,
    y = "Mean log(RT) (participant-weighted)", 
    x = "Rotation angle (degrees)",
    colour = "Strategy", fill = "Strategy"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Strategy Use Across Age Groups {.appendix #apx-strategy-age-group}
We examined whether the distribution of strategy clusters varied across age groups (@fig-strategy-by-age). This analysis is purely descriptive — cell sizes are too small for formal inferential testing, and the cluster solution itself carries the caveats described above. With those caveats in mind, a descriptive pattern is nonetheless visible. The proportion of children assigned to the Ineffective Strategies cluster declined substantially with age, from `r get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100`% in the youngest group (ages 5–8.3) to `r get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100`% (ages 8.3–10.6) and `r get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100`% 
(ages 10.6–13.7). This was accompanied by a corresponding increase in the Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) cluster, from 
`r get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)") * 100`% to `r get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)") * 100`% and `r get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)") * 100`%. By contrast, the proportion assigned to the Mental Rotation cluster remained stable across age groups (`r get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Mental Rotation") * 100`%, 
`r get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Mental Rotation") * 100`%, `r get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Mental Rotation") * 100`%). The primary developmental shift thus appears to be a move away from task disengagement toward effective feature-matching engagement profiles, with the proportion using analog rotation remaining comparatively stable across this age range.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strategy-by-age
#| fig-align: "center"
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "**Strategy cluster proportions by age group.**"

strategy_by_age %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = prop, fill = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = my_colors,
                    labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Age group (years)",
       y = "Proportion",
       fill = "Strategy") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
  
# Dimensionality Reduction Checks {.appendix #apx-dimreduc}
To validate the cluster structure, we examined whether the three-cluster solution was recoverable using alternative dimensionality reduction methods: PCA (@fig-pca-check), t-SNE (@fig-tsne-check), and UMAP (@fig-umap-check). PCA loadings were also inspected to characterize the underlying feature structure (@fig-pca-loadings).

Results were consistent across all three methods in one key respect: the Ineffective Strategies group was clearly and reliably separated from the two effective strategy groups, appearing as a distinct region in all three projections — the top-left in the t-SNE, the negative end of PC1 in the PCA, and the bottom-left in the UMAP. This convergent separation provides strong evidence that this group occupies a genuinely distinct region of the feature space. The boundary between the Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) groups was, however, substantially less clear. Green and blue points overlapped considerably across all three visualizations, suggesting these two groups may represent ends of a continuum rather than fully discrete clusters — a finding consistent with the silhouette analysis favoring k = 2.

Inspection of the PCA loadings offered interpretive support for the feature set. PC1 loaded positively on Baseline Speed, Learning Rate, and Absolute Slope, and negatively on Instability, reflecting a general processing efficiency dimension: children who respond faster, improve more across trials, and show less trial-to-trial noise score higher on this component. PC2 loaded most strongly on Relative Slope and Absolute Slope — both positive — and negatively on Learning Rate, reflecting a rotation cost dimension that is largely independent of general speed. The fact that these two components map onto theoretically meaningful and distinct dimensions provides confidence that the clustering features are not redundant.
```{r}
#| label: fig-tsne-check
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**t-SNE visualization of strategy clusters.** The Ineffective Strategies group forms a distinct region in the top-left, while the Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching groups show considerable overlap in the central and right regions, suggesting softer boundaries between the two effective strategy groups."

tsne_input <- analysis_data %>%
    select(run_id, Learning_Rate, Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Instability) %>%
    distinct() %>% 
    na.omit()

set.seed(42) 
tsne_result <- Rtsne(
    as.matrix(tsne_input %>% select(-run_id)), 
    dims = 2, 
    perplexity = 30, 
    verbose = FALSE, 
    max_iter = 500
)

tsne_plot_data <- tsne_input %>%
    mutate(
        tSNE_1 = tsne_result$Y[,1],
        tSNE_2 = tsne_result$Y[,2]
    ) %>%
    left_join(analysis_data %>% select(run_id, Strategy_Label), by = "run_id")

ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = tSNE_1, y = tSNE_2, color = Strategy_Label)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) +
    labs(
        title = NULL,
        x = "Dimension 1",
        y = "Dimension 2",
        color = "Strategy"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-check
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**PCA projection of the five clustering features coloured by strategy group.** The Ineffective Strategies group separates clearly along PC1, while the Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching groups overlap along both components."

pca_result <- prcomp(tsne_input %>% select(-run_id), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pca_plot_data <- tsne_input %>%
    mutate(PC1 = pca_result$x[,1], PC2 = pca_result$x[,2]) %>%
    left_join(analysis_data %>% select(run_id, Strategy_Label), by = "run_id")

ggplot(pca_plot_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Strategy_Label)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) +
    labs(
        title = NULL,
        x = "PC1",
        y = "PC2",
        color = "Strategy"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-loadings
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**PCA loadings for PC1 and PC2.** PC1 reflects a general processing efficiency dimension, loading positively on Baseline Speed, Learning Rate, and Absolute Slope, and negatively on Instability. PC2 reflects a rotation cost dimension, driven primarily by Relative and Absolute Slope."

loadings_df <- as.data.frame(pca_result$rotation) %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Angle_Condition")

loadings_long <- loadings_df %>%
  select(Angle_Condition, PC1, PC2) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(PC1, PC2), 
    names_to = "Principal_Component", 
    values_to = "Loading"
  )

ggplot(loadings_long, aes(
    x = Loading, 
    y = reorder_within(Angle_Condition, Loading, Principal_Component), 
    fill = Loading > 0
  )) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Principal_Component, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = pal$blue, "FALSE" = pal$red)) +
  labs(
    title    = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL,
    x = "Loading Weight",
    y = "Feature"
  ) +
  theme(
    #strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    #panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-umap-check
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
```

# Full 0–360° Angle Functions check {.appendix #apx-360-angle}
The primary analyses modeled angular disparity as the shortest path to upright, capped at 180°, on the assumption that participants take the most efficient route when rotating stimuli. To test this assumption, we re-ran the clustering using full 0–360° rotation angles and plotted RT and accuracy functions across the complete angular range (@fig-rt-angle-by-strategy-360, @fig-accuracy-angle-by-strategy-360). We verified that the angular disparity variable was correctly computed, confirming that full rotation angles were accurately recoded to their shortest-path equivalents (e.g., a 320° rotation has a disparity of 40°).

The results were broadly consistent with the disparity-based analyses and provided direct support for the shortest-path assumption. Both the Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) groups showed RT functions that increased from 20° to a peak around 200–240°, then declined as angles approached 320°, forming the expected near-symmetric inverted-U around 180°. This pattern is what would be predicted if participants always rotate via the shorter available path, and would not be expected under a fixed-direction rotation strategy.

The flipping signature observed in the Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) group was again evident in the full-angle data: their RT function rose more steeply than the Mental Rotation group and remained elevated through 240° before declining, consistent with a strategy that exploits reflective symmetry at high disparities. Accuracy for both effective strategy groups showed a corresponding U-shaped function, declining to a minimum around 160–200° before recovering at higher angles, with the Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) group maintaining the highest accuracy throughout. The Ineffective Strategies group again showed a broadly decreasing RT function across the full angular range, with accuracy remaining near chance at peak angles and showing only a modest recovery above 240°, further supporting the interpretation that these children are not engaging with the spatial structure of the items.

```{r}
#| label: robustness-check-all-angles
#| results: "hide"

# NOTE: all objects in this and subsequent 360° chunks use _360 suffixes to avoid overwriting main analysis objects. These chunks must remain the
# last substantive analysis chunks in the document.

mrot_rich_data_360 <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  rename(ang_disparity = angle,
         angle = angle_full) %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(ang_disparity)),
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

contrasts(mrot_rich_data_360$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_rich_data_360$stimulus))

m_rich_360 <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_s * stimulus + trial_s +
    (1 + angle_s + trial_s | run_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mrot_rich_data_360,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 20000))
)

ran_effs_360 <- ranef(m_rich_360)$run_id %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("run_id") %>%
  rename(
    int_dev   = `(Intercept)`,
    slope_dev = angle_s,
    trial_dev = trial_s
  )

fix_int_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["(Intercept)"]
fix_ang_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["angle_s"]
fix_tri_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["trial_s"]

rich_features_raw_360 <- ran_effs_360 %>%
  mutate(
    Baseline_Speed = fix_int_360 + int_dev,
    Abs_Slope      = fix_ang_360 + slope_dev,
    Rel_Slope      = Abs_Slope / Baseline_Speed,
    Learning_Rate  = fix_tri_360 + trial_dev
  )

mrot_rich_data_360$resid <- residuals(m_rich_360)

instability_data_360 <- mrot_rich_data_360 %>%
  group_by(run_id) %>%
  summarise(
    Instability = sd(resid, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

rich_features_final_360 <- rich_features_raw_360 %>%
  left_join(instability_data_360, by = "run_id") %>%
  left_join(ability_run, by = "run_id") %>%
  mutate(Site = site_label) %>%
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Baseline_Speed, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

# Check: ang_disparity should never exceed 180
summary(mrot_rich_data_360$ang_disparity)

# Spot check a few items
mrot_rich_data_360 %>%
  select(item, item_original, angle, ang_disparity) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  arrange(item_original) %>%
  head(20)
  
```

####################### ROBUSTNESS CHECK - BOOTSTRAPPING ##########################
```{r}
#| label: cluster-stability-bootstrap
#| include: false
#| eval: false

vars   <- c("Baseline_Speed", "Rel_Slope", "Abs_Slope", "Instability", "Learning_Rate")
k      <- 3
B      <- 500
nstart <- 25
set.seed(123)

df_full <- analysis_data %>%
  select(user_id, Strategy_Label, all_of(vars)) %>%
  distinct(user_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(if_all(all_of(vars), is.finite)) %>%
  mutate(
    Strategy_Label = factor(
      Strategy_Label,
      levels = names(my_colors)   
    )
  )

stopifnot(nlevels(df_full$Strategy_Label) == 3)
stopifnot(n_distinct(df_full$user_id) == nrow(df_full))

ref_levels <- levels(df_full$Strategy_Label)
y_ref      <- df_full$Strategy_Label
ids        <- df_full$user_id
n          <- nrow(df_full)

# scaling: lock to full-sample mean/sd so bootstrap runs are comparable
mu  <- df_full %>% summarise(across(all_of(vars), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))) %>% as.list()
sdv <- df_full %>% summarise(across(all_of(vars), \(x) sd(x,   na.rm = TRUE))) %>% as.list()

X_full <- df_full %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(vars), ~ (. - mu[[cur_column()]]) / sdv[[cur_column()]])) %>%
  select(all_of(vars)) %>%
  as.matrix()

# helpers
ARI <- function(a, b) {
  a <- as.integer(factor(a))
  b <- as.integer(factor(b))
  tab <- table(a, b)
  n <- sum(tab)
  if (n <= 1) return(NA_real_)
  comb2    <- function(x) x * (x - 1) / 2
  sum_ij   <- sum(comb2(tab))
  sum_i    <- sum(comb2(rowSums(tab)))
  sum_j    <- sum(comb2(colSums(tab)))
  expected <- (sum_i * sum_j) / comb2(n)
  max_idx  <- 0.5 * (sum_i + sum_j)
  denom    <- max_idx - expected
  if (denom == 0) return(NA_real_)
  (sum_ij - expected) / denom
}

jaccard <- function(set_a, set_b) {
  inter <- length(intersect(set_a, set_b))
  uni   <- length(union(set_a, set_b))
  if (uni == 0) NA_real_ else inter / uni
}

all_perms_3 <- list(
  c(1,2,3), c(1,3,2),
  c(2,1,3), c(2,3,1),
  c(3,1,2), c(3,2,1)
)

# Match bootstrap cluster IDs to reference labels by maximum membership overlap
best_perm_by_overlap <- function(cl_hat, y_ref, ref_levels, all_perms_3) {
  tab    <- table(cl_hat, factor(y_ref, levels = ref_levels))
  scores <- sapply(all_perms_3, function(p) sum(tab[cbind(1:3, p)]))
  all_perms_3[[which.max(scores)]]
}

# reference k-means (reproduces clustering-execution exactly)
# UPDATED: label assignment now mirrors the two-step logic in clustering-execution:
#   step 1 — lowest mean ability  → "Ineffective Strategies"
#   step 2 — of the remainder, flatter Rel_Slope → "Other Effective...", 
#             steeper → "Mental Rotation"
# We use this to build ref_centers aligned to ref_levels.

# need ability for label assignment (not a clustering var, so grab separately)
ability_lookup <- df_full %>%
  left_join(analysis_data %>% distinct(user_id, ability), by = "user_id")

set.seed(123)
km_ref <- kmeans(X_full, centers = k, nstart = nstart)
cl_ref <- km_ref$cluster

# replicate the production label-assignment rule on the reference run
cluster_stats_ref <- tibble(
  cluster      = 1:k,
  mean_ability = tapply(ability_lookup$ability, cl_ref, mean, na.rm = TRUE),
  mean_rel_slope = tapply(df_full$Rel_Slope,   cl_ref, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
)

low_eff_id_ref  <- cluster_stats_ref %>% arrange(mean_ability) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(cluster)
effective_ref   <- cluster_stats_ref %>% filter(cluster != low_eff_id_ref) %>% arrange(mean_rel_slope)
analytical_id_ref <- effective_ref %>% slice(1) %>% pull(cluster)
holistic_id_ref   <- effective_ref %>% slice(2) %>% pull(cluster)

# map cluster integer to ref_levels index (used to order ref_centers rows)
label_order_ref <- integer(k)
label_order_ref[low_eff_id_ref]   <- which(ref_levels == "Ineffective Strategies")
label_order_ref[analytical_id_ref] <- which(ref_levels == "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)")
label_order_ref[holistic_id_ref]   <- which(ref_levels == "Mental Rotation")

# ref_centers[i, ] corresponds to ref_levels[i]
ref_centers <- km_ref$centers[order(label_order_ref), , drop = FALSE]

# bootstrap loop
res <- map_dfr(1:B, function(b) {

  set.seed(1000 + b)

  idx        <- sample.int(n, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  idx_unique <- unique(idx)

  tab_ref_unique <- table(factor(y_ref[idx_unique], levels = ref_levels))
  min_ref_unique <- min(tab_ref_unique)
  min_ref_prop   <- min_ref_unique / length(idx_unique)
  n_unique       <- length(idx_unique)

  X_b <- X_full[idx, , drop = FALSE]
  km  <- kmeans(X_b, centers = k, nstart = nstart)

  # assign all full-sample participants to nearest bootstrap center
  centers_b <- km$centers
  dists <- sapply(1:k, function(j) {
    rowSums((X_full - matrix(centers_b[j, ],
                             nrow = nrow(X_full), ncol = ncol(X_full),
                             byrow = TRUE))^2)
  })
  cl_hat <- max.col(-dists)

  # resolve label switching via maximum overlap with reference labels
  perm  <- best_perm_by_overlap(cl_hat, y_ref, ref_levels, all_perms_3)
  y_hat <- factor(ref_levels[perm[cl_hat]], levels = ref_levels)

  ari <- ARI(y_ref, y_hat)

  # per-cluster Jaccard
  jac <- map_dbl(ref_levels, function(lab) {
    jaccard(ids[y_ref == lab], ids[y_hat == lab])
  })
  names(jac) <- paste0("J_", make.names(ref_levels))

  # mean centroid displacement vs reference
  centers_b_aligned <- centers_b[perm, , drop = FALSE]
  center_shift      <- mean(sqrt(rowSums((centers_b_aligned - ref_centers)^2)))

  tibble(
    replicate      = b,
    ARI            = ari,
    n_unique       = n_unique,
    min_ref_unique = min_ref_unique,
    min_ref_prop   = min_ref_prop,
    center_shift   = center_shift,
    !!!as.list(jac)
  )
})

# summaries
stability_summary <- res %>%
  summarise(
    B                   = n(),
    ARI_median          = median(ARI, na.rm = TRUE),
    ARI_IQR             = IQR(ARI, na.rm = TRUE),
    center_shift_median = median(center_shift, na.rm = TRUE),
    center_shift_IQR    = IQR(center_shift, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(starts_with("J_"),
           list(median = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
                IQR    = ~ IQR(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  )

stability_summary

ari_tail <- res %>%
  summarise(
    pct_ARI_below_0.70 = mean(ARI < 0.70, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_ARI_below_0.60 = mean(ARI < 0.60, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    min_ARI            = min(ARI, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ari_tail
```

```{r}
# ARI distribution across bootstrap resamples
ggplot(res, aes(x = ARI)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(res$ARI, na.rm = TRUE), 
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "ARI (vs reference clustering)", y = "Count",
       title = paste0("Bootstrap stability (B = ", nrow(res), ")"),
       subtitle = paste0("Median ARI = ", round(median(res$ARI, na.rm = TRUE), 3)))

# Per-cluster Jaccard
res %>%
  select(replicate, starts_with("J_")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-replicate, names_to = "Cluster", values_to = "Jaccard") %>%
  mutate(Cluster = str_remove(Cluster, "^J_")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Jaccard, fill = Cluster)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ Cluster, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Jaccard index", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

####################### ROBUSTNESS CHECK - WITHIN PERSON STRATEGY SWITCHING (DORIA'S ANALYSIS) ##########################

### Strategy Stability Analysis (Split-Half Reliability)

To investigate whether children consistently use a single cognitive strategy throughout the task or switch strategies over time (e.g., discovering a shortcut), we performed a **Split-Half Reliability Analysis**.

**Methodology:**
We partitioned each participant's data into two sequential halves: the first 50% of trials (Early Phase) and the last 50% of trials (Late Phase). For each half, we estimated a "Raw Slope" using a simple linear regression of reaction time on angle (`log_rt ~ angle`). This slope serves as a proxy for the participant's rotation strategy during that specific period. 

We then correlated the *First Half Slope* with the *Second Half Slope* to quantify stability. A high correlation ($r \approx 1$) would indicate a fixed strategy, while a low correlation ($r \approx 0$) suggests dynamic behavior or strategy switching.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strategy-switching
#| fig-cap: "Strategy Stability: Comparison of Rotation Slope in First Half vs. Second Half of trials. Points below the diagonal suggest a switch to a flatter strategy (e.g., discovering the shortcut)."
#| eval: false

# 1. Split Data into Halves
# We determine the midpoint trial for each user
split_data <- mrot_rich_data %>%
  group_by(user_id) %>%
  mutate(
    Midpoint = median(trial_number, na.rm = TRUE),
    Half = ifelse(trial_number <= Midpoint, "First_Half", "Second_Half")
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Filter out bad data points just to be safe
  filter(is.finite(log_rt), is.finite(angle))

# 2. Calculate Simple Slope for Each Half (Using simple lm per subject)
# This is a fast proxy for the complex mixed-model slope
slope_stability <- split_data %>%
  group_by(user_id, Half) %>%
  summarise(
    # We only care about the slope (coefficient for angle)
    # We use a safe lm() call wrapped in tryCatch to handle kids with too few trials
    Raw_Slope = tryCatch(
      #coef(lm(log_rt ~ angle, data = pick(everything())))["angle"], 
      # Use distance from 0 so the slope represents 'cost of rotation'
  coef(lm(log_rt ~ pmin(angle, 360 - angle), data = pick(everything())))[2],
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Reshape to Wide Format (Columns: Slope_First, Slope_Second)
  pivot_wider(names_from = Half, values_from = Raw_Slope, names_prefix = "Slope_") %>%
  # Join with our Final Strategy Labels to color-code
  left_join(analysis_data %>% select(user_id, Strategy_Label), by = "user_id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Label), !is.na(Slope_First_Half), !is.na(Slope_Second_Half))

# 3. Calculate Correlation (Quantify Stability)
correlation <- cor(slope_stability$Slope_First_Half, slope_stability$Slope_Second_Half, use = "complete.obs")

# 4. Visualization
ggplot(slope_stability, aes(x = Slope_First_Half, y = Slope_Second_Half, color = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") + # The "Stability Line"
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Strategy Switching Check (Split-Half Reliability)",
    subtitle = paste0("Correlation between halves: r = ", round(correlation, 2), 
                      ". Points below diagonal = Strategy became flatter (faster)."),
    x = "Slope (First Half of Trials)",
    y = "Slope (Second Half of Trials)"
  ) +
  coord_fixed() # Keeps the aspect ratio square so the diagonal is 45 degrees
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Doria's original code for examining up to 360 
mrot_rich_data <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus = str_extract(item, "^[a-z]+"),
    
    # 1. Extract the base angle (e.g., 40)
    base_angle = as.integer(str_extract(item, "\\d+")), 
    
    # 2. Detect if the original item was a "Negative/Counter-Clockwise" rotation
    # Looking for 'rn' prefix in item_original (e.g., rn040)
    is_ccw = str_detect(item_original, "^rn"),
    
    # 3. RECONSTRUCT the full 0-360 angle
    angle = ifelse(is_ccw, 360 - base_angle, base_angle),
    
    # 4. Calculate shortest distance to center (disparity) for the model
    # This ensures the model still measures 'Rotation Cost' correctly
    ang_disparity = pmin(angle, 360 - angle),
    
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    # SCALE THE DISPARITY, NOT THE RAW ANGLE
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(ang_disparity)), 
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

#  Issues: the above code is only only catches rabbit counter-clockwise items (rn040, rn080 etc.), and misses duck and shape items. It is also not necessary to deconstruct item_original as the info. we need is already there. item_original already contains the full angle directly (e.g., an11240 = 240).
```
